strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-explored gap in sleep representation learning by explicitly modeling both micro-structure (second-scale biosignal morphology) and macro-structure (full-night sleep architecture) within a unified hierarchical framework, rather than the epoch-level focus of prior sleep foundation models (SleepFM, OSF, Sleep2Vec, etc.).

Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning (DGCL) is a well-motivated and reasonably novel idea: using objective, scalable metadata (age, sex, BMI) as a supervisory signal for macro-structure pretraining sidesteps the well-documented inter-scorer variability and evolving AASM guideline issues that plague label-based sleep staging supervision. The empirical visualization in Figure 4 supporting the demographic-macrostructure link is a nice motivating analysis.

Pretraining corpus is large and diverse (>20,000 PSG recordings, 158K hours, 8+ cohorts across multiple countries/manufacturers), and the paper evaluates on both in-distribution (SHHS1, KISS) and fully held-out external cohorts (CFS, SOF, ISRUC), which is a meaningful test of generalization.

Broad evaluation suite: sleep staging, SDB segmentation, disease prediction (via Cox PH/C-index), few-shot adaptation, and an ablation program covering core components, demographic factors, cycle length, Macro-Encoder architecture choice, and alternative pretraining objectives (SimCLR, DINO) — this is a fairly comprehensive empirical treatment for a systems-level contribution.

Reasonable attention to reproducibility (detailed architecture tables, hyperparameters, dataset preprocessing, channel/sampling-rate tables in the appendix) and to fairness/ethics considerations (subgroup analysis for demographic bias in Appendix E, explicit Impact Statement discussion).
weaknesses: The abstract/main text claim that SleepMaMi 'outperforms or matches state-of-the-art foundation models' is accurate only relative to other foundation models; comparisons to fully supervised, task-specialized models (Table 17, 19, appendix) reveal SleepMaMi trailing considerably in several cases (e.g., SDB segmentation Macro-F1 60.6 vs. AIX's 74.6 on SHHS1; sleep staging accuracy gaps of 1–5 points vs. SleePyCo/DistillSleep). This important caveat is relegated to the appendix rather than discussed prominently in the main paper, giving a somewhat inflated impression of the method's absolute standing.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the paper (pretraining or downstream fine-tuning); all reported numbers appear to be single runs, which weakens confidence in the many close margins observed (e.g., DGCL vs. SimCLR/DINO ablation differs by only ~0.1–0.2 points, Table 16).

Baseline coverage is inconsistent across tasks: disease prediction (Table 3) is compared only against SleepFM-Disease, omitting the time-series and EEG foundation model baselines used elsewhere, which limits the strength of the disease-prediction contribution claim. Similarly, LaBraM is dropped from CFS/SOF sleep-staging and SDB tables without clear justification.

SDB segmentation and staging results occasionally show accuracy decreasing while Macro-F1 increases relative to baselines (e.g., SOF SDB: SleepMaMi accuracy 70.2 vs. UniTS 90.6, though Macro-F1 favors SleepMaMi), suggesting the model may be trading off majority-class performance for minority-class sensitivity; this behavior deserves more direct discussion/analysis (e.g., calibration, precision-recall trade-off) rather than being framed solely as a class-imbalance artifact.

The demographic distance function underlying DGCL (equal weighting of z-scored age and BMI plus a fixed sex penalty) is acknowledged as empirically chosen but not rigorously validated against alternative formulations; the ablation against SimCLR/DINO tests different learning objectives but does not probe sensitivity to the distance metric itself, leaving the core design choice under-justified.

Reproducibility is nominally supported by extensive appendix detail, but the actual code/checkpoint URL is left blank in the submission ('Our source code and checkpoint are available at'), so the promised release cannot be verified at review time.

The technical architecture, while carefully engineered, largely combines existing building blocks (MAE, contrastive learning, MoE, RoPE/SwiGLU/RMSNorm Transformers, bidirectional Mamba) rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms; the primary originality lies in the systems-level integration and the DGCL objective, which is a reasonable but incremental contribution for a top-tier venue.

Several of the comparator citations (Thapa et al. 2026 Nature Medicine, Huang et al. 2026 Nature Communications, Yuan et al. 2026 ICLR, Shuai et al. 2026 ICML, Lee et al. 2026 ICLR) are dated 2026, which, while plausibly valid as concurrently accepted work, makes independent verification of claimed baseline results difficult for reviewers at this stage.

strengths: Novel and reasonably well-motivated hierarchical dual-encoder design that explicitly separates sleep micro-structure (short-term signal morphology) from macro-structure (full-night architecture), addressing a real gap in the sleep foundation model literature where prior work (e.g., SleepFM) focuses mainly on local/epoch-level representations.

The proposed Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning (DGCL) objective is a creative way to obtain a noise-free, scalable supervisory signal for macro-structure learning without relying on subjective/expert-scored labels, and is supported by clear exploratory evidence (Figures 4, 8, 9) showing that sleep stage trajectories differ systematically by age, sex, and BMI.

Large-scale, multi-dataset pretraining corpus (>20K recordings, 158K hours across 7 public cohorts) with careful preprocessing and channel harmonization, which is a nontrivial engineering contribution and improves the credibility of claimed generalizability.

Reasonably comprehensive downstream evaluation spanning sleep staging, SDB segmentation, disease risk prediction (Cox PH), few-shot adaptation, and demographic probing, providing a multi-faceted view of representation quality rather than a single task.

Useful ablations (Table 11, Table 12) isolating the contribution of shared/private encoders, MAE, CL, large-scale pretraining, and DGCL, plus per-attribute analysis of which demographic signals (age/sex/BMI) help most.
Good documentation of architecture hyperparameters, training schedules, and dataset statistics in the appendix, which aids reproducibility even without released code.
weaknesses: Results are inconsistent across datasets and tasks in ways not fully resolved: on KISS, a generic time-series model (MOMENT) outperforms SleepMaMi on sleep staging, and on SHHS1 SDB segmentation UniTS achieves higher raw accuracy; the paper's explanation (Compumedics vs. Nox/Embla hardware distribution shift) is speculative and not empirically tested (e.g., no hardware-stratified ablation or domain adaptation experiment).

In the disease-prediction comparison (Table 3), SleepMaMi actually underperforms SleepFM-Disease on 3 of 6 outcomes (CVD death, CHD death, Stroke), yet the text frames this as 'comparable performance' without a more calibrated discussion of when/why the macro-structure signal helps or hurts.

The added value of DGCL specifically (as opposed to simply having more pretraining data and a Mamba-based macro-encoder) is only weakly isolated: Table 12 ablation trained solely on SHHS1 shows only ~1 percentage point gain from full DGCL (79.8% to 80.7%), which is a fairly marginal improvement and raises questions about how much of the large jump in Table 11 (79.8% to 81.9%) is attributable to DGCL versus other confounded factors such as increased Macro-Encoder capacity or additional Mamba layers.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported for any experiment; all comparisons rely on single-run point estimates, which is a significant limitation given several close margins (e.g., SDB accuracy differences on SHHS1 between SleepMaMi and SleepFM/UniTS).

Baseline comparisons may not be fully controlled: SleepFM-Disease is evaluated at a different sampling rate (256 Hz) than SleepMaMi's pipeline (100 Hz) per the baseline's specific requirements, which could confound the comparison, and no more recent or stronger sleep-specific SSL baselines beyond SleepFM/SleepFM-Disease are included.

Evaluation is dominated by linear probing; while this is reasonable for representation-quality assessment, the paper does not explore full fine-tuning (except briefly in the few-shot ISRUC setting, and even there only against SleepFM-Disease, omitting MOMENT/UniTS which were sometimes competitive earlier).

There is no explicit Limitations section, and ethical/fairness considerations around using demographic attributes (age, sex, BMI) as training signal for a clinical model are not discussed at all — e.g., potential propagation of demographic bias into downstream disease-risk predictions, or fairness concerns for underrepresented subgroups (the pretraining cohort skews heavily male in some datasets, e.g., MrOS is 100% male), which is a notable omission for a health-related foundation model.

No statement on code or model release, which combined with the complexity of the architecture (MoE, private-shared transformers, bi-directional Mamba, hierarchical patch merging) may hinder independent reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameter tables.
